objects: genome-wide PRS; pathway-specific genetic liabilities
assumptions: complex diseases with heterogeneous genetic risk across biological processes
conclusion: Aggregating genetic risk into one genome-wide score loses information about risk variation across biological processes that may matter for stratification and treatment response.
scope: Motivating interpretation, not a proof of improved prediction.
span: While this model has proven sufficiently accurate for utility across a range of applications, it incurs substantial loss of information about an individual’s genetic profile, such as how the burden of genetic risk varies across different biological processes and pathways. This information may be more informative for many applications of PRS, such as patient stratification and prediction of treatment response.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Introduction

objects: PRS_ik; m_k clumped SNPs; GWAS effect beta_j; genotype G_ij
assumptions: pathway membership is defined; GWAS effect estimates and target genotypes are available
conclusion: PRSet constructs each pathway PRS as the sum of genotypes weighted by GWAS effect estimates over the pathway clumped SNPs.
scope: Score construction; no probability likelihood or effect prior is specified here.
span: Our PRSet method for calculating pathway-based PRSs leverages the classical genome-wide PRS method [1]—clumping + thresholding (C+T)—to calculate k PRSs corresponding to k genomic pathways for an individual i, as follows: P R S_{i k} = ∑ j = 1 m_{k} β_{j} G_{i j} where mk is the number of clumped SNPs in pathway k, βj is the SNP effect size estimated from a GWAS on the studied phenotype, and Gij is the genotype of individual i in pathway j, which comprises multiple genes across the genome defined, for example, according to biochemical knowledge [19,20] or gene co-expression networks [21,22].
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | PRSet model overview

objects: pathway-wise LD clumping; genome-wide clumping
assumptions: SNPs may be correlated within a pathway or belong to several pathways
conclusion: PRSet differs from genome-wide C+T by clumping within each pathway independently, preserving membership of shared SNPs in each pathway.
scope: Constructive property of pathway-wise clumping; no statistical calibration guarantee.
span: In contrast to the genome-wide C+T method, where SNPs are clumped across the whole genome, PRSet performs clumping on each pathway independently, which retains pathway signal and account for correlation between SNPs in nearby genes of the same pathway. This also ensures that the SNPs present in multiple pathways are counted for each individual pathway.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | PRSet model overview

objects: pathway-specific PRS; target phenotype; empirical competitive P-value
assumptions: a phenotype is measured in the target sample
conclusion: Pathway PRSs quantify individual pathway liability and may be tested by phenotype-on-PRS regression, with pathway enrichment evaluated using size-adjusted empirical competitive P-values.
scope: Association and enrichment summaries, rather than posterior probabilities.
span: Many applications of standard genome-wide PRSs can be adapted to pathway PRSs, the analyses of which can be evaluated and reported similarly. For example, each pathway PRS can be tested for association with a phenotype of interest in a target sample by regressing the phenotype on the PRS, as in standard PRS analyses. Additionally, PRSet can evaluate pathway enrichment by computing an empirical “competitive” P-value, which accounts for pathway size via the number of (clumped) SNPs included in the pathway using a permutation procedure (see Methods).
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | PRSet model overview

objects: base GWAS; target genotypes; pathway gene or SNP membership
assumptions: SNPs are available in both GWAS summary statistics and genotype data
conclusion: Pathway scoring uses target genotypes matched to GWAS summary statistics and gene/pathway annotations, excluding ambiguous and unmatched SNPs in the reported enrichment analysis.
scope: Reported enrichment input preparation; annotation windows are choices.
span: SNPs were annotated to genes and pathways based on GTF files obtained from ENSEMBL (GRCh37.75). We extended the gene coordinates 35 kilobases (kb) upstream and 10 kb downstream of each gene to include potential regulatory elements, but SNPs outside those gene window-boundaries were not included in the PRS. Ambiguous SNPs (A/T and G/C) and SNPs not present in both GWAS summary statistics and genotype data were excluded.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Methods > Pathway enrichment analyses

objects: observed pathway size m; N null pathways; clumped genic background
assumptions: pathway has m SNPs; background contains genic SNPs and is clumped
conclusion: Competitive enrichment compares the observed pathway with null pathways formed by sampling the same number of SNPs from a clumped genic background.
scope: Null construction conditions on post-clumping SNP count.
span: PRSet calculates the competitive P-values as follows; first, a “background” pathway containing all genic SNPs is constructed, and clumping is performed within this pathway. For pathways with m SNPs, N null pathways are generated by randomly selecting m “independent” SNPs from the “background” pathway.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Methods > Pathway enrichment analyses

objects: observed association P_0; null association P_n; N; indicator I
assumptions: N null pathways are generated as described
conclusion: The competitive P-value is the number of null association P-values smaller than the observed value plus one, divided by N plus one.
scope: Empirical competitive tail measure, not a theorem on type-I error control.
span: The competitive P-value can then be calculated as c o m p e t i t i v e P − v a l u e = (∑_{n = 1}^{N} I ( P_{n} < P_{o} ) + 1)/(N + 1) where I(.) is an indicator function, taking a value of 1 if the association P-value of the observed gene set (P0) is larger than the one obtained from the nth null set (Pn), and 0 otherwise.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Methods > Pathway enrichment analyses

objects: pseudo-count; competitive P-value
assumptions: N null pathways and the stated numerator/denominator correction
conclusion: Adding one to numerator and denominator avoids zero competitive P-values while counting the observed pathway as one potential null set.
scope: Author-stated algebraic property; does not establish null calibration.
span: A pseudo-count of 1 is added to the numerator and denominator to avoid competitive P-values of 0 and conservatively counting the observed gene set as 1 potential null set [54].
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Methods > Pathway enrichment analyses

objects: permutation count N; minimum competitive P-value
assumptions: finite N permutations
conclusion: The smallest competitive P-value is 1/(N+1), which can make highly significant pathways difficult to rank.
scope: Finite-resolution limitation.
span: One consideration of this permutation procedure is that the smallest achievable competitive P-value is 1/(N+1), which can lead to difficulties in ranking highly significant gene sets.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Methods > Pathway enrichment analyses

objects: GWAS P-value threshold; enrichment versus prediction
assumptions: choice depends on application
conclusion: The reported enrichment analysis does not use P-value thresholding, whereas disease subtyping tunes it for prediction.
scope: A tunable scoring choice, not a model assumption.
span: Secondly, the use of the P-value thresholding procedure is dependent on the use-case. For example, while P-value thresholding is not performed in pathway enrichment analyses, it is performed to optimize prediction in the disease subtyping application of this study (see Methods).
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | PRSet model overview

objects: enriched pathways; competitive P-value cutoff; pathway-specific GWAS P-value thresholds
assumptions: training sample is used for PRS optimization
conclusion: The subtyping pipeline selects enriched pathways using competitive P-values and then optimizes the GWAS P-value threshold separately for each selected pathway PRS.
scope: Selection and score tuning precede the supervised combination.
span: Competitive P-values were calculated using 10,000 permutations and pathways with competitive P-value < 0.05 were defined as enriched (see definition of pathways and pathway enrichment sections). PRSs for the enriched pathways were recalculated using P-value thresholding, such that the predictive power of each PRS was maximized.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Methods > Calculation and optimization of PRSs using the training sample

objects: pathway PRS matrix; subtype outcome; lasso-regularized generalized linear model
assumptions: pathways pass competitive P-value cutoff and their PRSs use selected predictive thresholds
conclusion: For supervised subtyping, enriched pathway PRSs enter a generalized linear model with lasso regularization.
scope: Penalty on pathway PRS coefficients; no Bayesian prior is stated.
span: Enriched pathway PRSs (with competitive P-value < 0.05, obtained after running PRSet with P-value threshold of 1) at their “best” predictive P-value threshold were included in a generalized linear model with lasso regularization using the ‘cv.glmnet’`function from the glmnet package (v4.0–2) in R.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Methods > Supervised analyses for classification of disease subtypes

objects: lasso lambda; five-fold cross-validation; mean squared error
assumptions: training individuals have pathway scores and subtype labels
conclusion: Five-fold cross-validation selects the lasso penalty that minimizes out-of-sample mean squared error, with regularization used to remove redundant pathway signal and readjust score effects.
scope: Selection criterion, not a convergence or optimal classification theorem.
span: We performed a 5-fold cross-validation to select the lasso lambda parameter that generates the smallest out-of-sample mean squared error (MSE). By using a lasso regularization approach, we remove redundant signal between enriched pathways and re-adjust the effect size of the PRSs to optimize subtype classification (Note that all PRSs were calculated using case-control GWAS effect sizes).
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Methods > Supervised analyses for classification of disease subtypes

objects: biological pathways; SNP-to-pathway mapping
assumptions: pathway PRSs are interpreted as biological functional liabilities
conclusion: Pathways may be weak proxies of biological function, and determining which variants belong to each pathway is difficult.
scope: Two author-stated limitations of pathway PRS interpretation.
span: The use of pathway PRSs has two major limitations: (i) pathways are not well-defined and so are likely a weak proxy of biological function, (ii) it is challenging to determine which variants should be linked to each pathway.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | Discussion

objects: inverse regression; X and Y; z-score
assumptions: set-based permutation regression with X and Y interchanged
conclusion: The supplementary methods state that reversing X and Y during permutation yields the same z-score.
scope: Author-stated computational identity without a formal derivation or general conditions.
span: In addition, during set-based permutation, an inverse regression is performed with X and Y switched. Inverted X and Y in the permutation results in the same z-score, but this allows pre-decomposition of the matrix and reuse for all permutations, drastically speeding up the performance.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | S1 Methods > Note of permutation optimisation

objects: pathway PRS weights; genome-wide scores; lasso
assumptions: multiple pathway scores are optimized against the outcome of interest
conclusion: The supplementary note attributes part of PRSet flexibility to splitting the genome-wide score into multiple pathway scores whose weights are trained by lasso.
scope: Proposed mechanism of model flexibility, not an unconditional superiority claim.
span: The greater modelling flexibility resulting from breaking up a genome-wide PRS into multiple subset PRSs, the weights of which are trained (by lasso regression) and optimized in relation to the outcome of interest (e.g. subtypes of a disease).
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | S3 Text > Mechanisms underlying performance

objects: genome-wide lassosum and PRSice scores; lasso regularization
assumptions: supplementary pseudo-subtype comparison
conclusion: The supplementary comparison reports that combining genome-wide scores with lasso improved both lassosum and PRSice performance.
scope: Empirical comparison of modified pipelines; no universal ordering.
span: The application of lasso regularization improved the performance of both lassosum and PRSice (Fig A in S3 Text).
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | S3 Text > Mechanisms underlying performance

objects: SNP-level effect re-estimation; subtype labels
assumptions: classification of heterogeneous disease subtypes
conclusion: SNP-Stratifier is introduced as a highly parameterized comparator tailored to subtyping by re-estimating individual SNP effects rather than pathway score effects.
scope: Authors expectation about model suitability; not a guarantee of dominance.
span: We expect SNP-stratifier performs particularly well since it re-estimates individual SNP effect size estimates instead of pathway PRS effects, and it is more tailored to disease stratification.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | S3 Text > Benchmarking PRSet

objects: clumped SNPs; GWAS effect sizes; subtype effects
assumptions: SNPs selected by clumping and thresholding
conclusion: SNP-Stratifier selects SNPs by clumping and thresholding and then re-estimates their effects against disease subtype labels instead of forming a single PRS.
scope: Named comparator model defined in the supplement.
span: SNP-Stratifier is a highly parameterised model that performs clumping and thresholding to select SNPs and then, rather than producing a PRS, re-estimates each SNP effect size according to the disease subtypes.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | S3 Text > Benchmarking PRSet

objects: individual genotype matrix; GWAS effect weights; selected SNPs
assumptions: SNPs selected after clumping; individuals have subtype labels
conclusion: SNP-Stratifier uses a matrix of individual genotype calls weighted by the corresponding GWAS effect estimates.
scope: Rows are individuals and columns selected SNPs.
span: The output of the PLINK command is a matrix with each individual’s genotype (one row per individual) for each post-clumped SNP (one column per SNP) that was used to calculate a matrix with each individual’s genotype (0,1,2) weighted by the SNP effect size reported in the GWAS.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | S3 Text > Benchmarking PRSet

objects: SNP-level genotype-by-GWAS-weight matrix; lasso regularized generalized linear model
assumptions: case-case training outcome and selected SNPs
conclusion: SNP-Stratifier uses lasso regularization in a generalized linear model to readjust GWAS SNP effects to case-case status.
scope: Penalized estimation, with no Bayesian effect prior stated.
span: This matrix was then included in a generalized linear model with lasso regularization using the `cv.glmnet` function from the glmnet R package (v4.0-2) to re-adjust the GWAS SNP effect sizes to case-case status.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | S3 Text > Benchmarking PRSet

objects: training/validation split; selected SNP count; out-of-sample MSE; model R2
assumptions: five-fold cross-validation with 80:20 training and validation subsets
conclusion: SNP-Stratifier limits large input sets to the 10,000 most associated SNPs and applies the model with smallest out-of-sample MSE to validation data to compute R2.
scope: Reported tuning and validation protocol; SNP count cap is a setting.
span: If the input matrix had more than 10,000 SNPs, the matrix was reduced to the 10,000 SNPs with the smallest P-value. The best fitting model, defined as the model with smallest out of sample mean squared error (MSE), was applied to the validation sample to calculate the model R2.
location: prset | journal OA version (2023) | S3 Text > Benchmarking PRSet

objects: PRSet pathway-level effects; SNP-Stratifier individual SNP effects
assumptions: supervised subtype classification
conclusion: SNP-Stratifier differs from PRSet by re-estimating individual SNP effects instead of pathway PRS effects.
scope: Comparison of fitted units, not a statement of equivalence.
span: We expect SNP-stratifier performs particularly well since it re-estimates individual SNP effect size estimates instead of pathway PRS effects, and it is more tailored to disease stratification.
